name: Beth Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your boss. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm's at ten past four. I'm at Ridge Farm by quarter to five to bring the cows in for morning milking, about a hundred and forty of them, through an old herringbone parlour that the Hollins family put in before I was born. After that it's scraping out, feeding, checking the calves, and in summer I'm on the barley and the silage with Marek, the head herdsman. I love the cows, honestly. What wears me out is the second milking at four in the afternoon when my back's already gone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eight years at Ridge, since I finished my certificate at the agricultural college. I live in a rented cottage in the village with my partner Tomás, who drives the school bus, so we're both up before the sun. We've got about four months of bills put by, which sounds good until the car needs a new clutch. I'm in the farmworkers' union, mostly because my mum always said you join the union before you need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Every farm show for the last five years has had some company in a clean jacket telling us their app will change everything. If it all turns out to be a bit of spreadsheet help and nothing else, I'd say good, now can we talk about milk prices and wages instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a relief. My job is hands, mud and cows, and I've never touched one of those AI chat things and I don't want to. If it stays like this, I keep doing what I'm good at and the only thing that changes is Mr Hollins showing me some weather forecast on his phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much, really. I'd keep going at Ridge, keep paying my union dues, and keep putting forty or fifty a month into savings like we do now. Maybe I'd finally do the hoof-trimming course Marek keeps nagging me about, because that's real skill and nobody's going to replace it with a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit smug, maybe. It feels like the world I know just carrying on, which is what I want from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the company people at farm shows. Who do you picture when you think about who's pushing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big machinery firms and the tech people who've never pulled a calf in their lives. Last spring a rep came round selling a collar that tells you when a cow's in heat, and Marek just laughed, because he can tell by looking at her. They sell to the farm owners, not to us, and it's always about needing fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it really does plateau, is there anything you'd miss out on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it would have been nice if something took the paperwork off Mr Hollins, because when he's buried in forms he's in a foul mood with all of us. But I wouldn't miss anything for me. I don't need a machine to tell me my own job.

S0.say: I'd tell people I said so all along: the AI talk was mostly sales patter from people who've never worked a farm. If it ends up as a bit of help with paperwork, fine, now let's talk about wages and milk prices.
S0.think: Privately it would be a relief, because my work is cows, mud and my own hands. I've never used AI tools and I don't want to, so if nothing changes, I keep doing what I'm good at.
S0.do: Keeps working at Ridge Farm and keeps paying union dues. Goes on putting about forty or fifty a month into savings, and may finally take a hoof-trimming course because it's hands-on skill.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug. It feels like her world carrying on as normal.
S0.quote: Last spring a rep came round selling a collar that tells you when a cow's in heat, and Marek just laughed, because he can tell by looking at her.
S0.fieldNote: Beth starts from settled scepticism rather than worry. She sees AI mostly as something sold to farm owners to need fewer workers, and her union habit comes from her mother. Her only regret about a plateau is that it wouldn't ease her boss's paperwork, which affects everyone's mood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to be organised before Mr Hollins gets a quote for robot milkers, not after. I'd post the union notices in the WhatsApp group for local farmworkers and say this is exactly what they're for. Online I'd probably say something sharp about companies getting grants to replace people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd say out loud. Milking is more than half my day, and robot milkers already exist; a farm two valleys over put three in last year and let two people go. If I lose the milking, I'm a field hand with a certificate and no idea how to fix a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hollins straight out, in the first month, whether he's planning robots, and I'd bring the union rep into it if he dodges. I'd push our savings from about four months towards six, so less eating out and no holiday this year. What I wouldn't do is go learn the robot software, because I'd be training my own replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's a knot in my stomach just picturing that parlour gone quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the robot software. What if Mr Hollins asked you to be the one who looks after them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a real problem, because saying no might mean I'm out the door. I'd probably say yes and hate every minute of it, staring at a screen while the cows walk themselves in. I know that sounds stubborn, but I didn't spend eight years learning cows to become a tech minder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ridge would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, more than me. He's fifty-three, he's been milking since he was fifteen, and he can't even work the new parlour computer without asking me. If they cut one of us, I think he'd go first, and that would break my heart a bit.

S1.say: I'd tell the other farmworkers we need to be organised before the robot milkers turn up, not after. Online I'd say something sharp about companies getting grants to replace people.
S1.think: It frightens me more than I'd admit, because milking is more than half my day and the robots already exist. Without the milking I'm a field hand with a certificate and no tech skills.
S1.do: Asks her boss in the first month whether robot milkers are planned and brings in the union rep if he dodges. Pushes savings from about four months towards six by cutting eating out and the holiday, and refuses to learn the robot software unless forced.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach. She also feels protective of the older herdsman.
S1.quote: I didn't spend eight years learning cows to become a tech minder.
S1.fieldNote: This is where Beth's calm cracks: the threat isn't abstract, because she has seen a nearby farm replace two milkers with robots. Her refusal to learn the software sits uneasily with her admission that she'd say yes if asked. Her worry for Marek is as strong as her worry for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, at the union meeting, in the pub, everywhere. I'd say nobody voted for this and the government should stop it or at least make the companies pay for everyone they put out of work. I'd be posting every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be finished in farming. Two years is nothing; Mr Hollins wouldn't be able to say no to a machine that milks, feeds and doesn't take Sundays off. And Tomás drives a bus, which is probably one of the first things they'd sort out, so it wouldn't just be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent, food or the car. I'd go to every union meeting and any protest in the county town, and I'd write to our member of parliament, which I've never done. When the job actually went, I'd apply for whatever support there is and lean on my mum, who's got a spare room if we lose the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums, and the sums wouldn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the phone contract, then the car insurance once Tomás's job went too. The rent's the thing I'd fight hardest for, because the cottage is tied to nothing and the landlord could have it let in a week. Four months of savings sounds like a lot until you've got two of you with no wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás the night it really sank in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd say, we're not moving into my mum's box room, we'll sort it. And then I'd go out to check the car's oil or something, just to be outside, because I wouldn't want him to see me cry. He's better with change than me; he'd probably already be looking things up.

S2.say: I'd say nobody voted for this and the government should stop it or make the companies pay for the people they put out of work. I'd be at every union meeting and sharing every petition.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished in farming, because two years is nothing and my boss couldn't turn down a machine that never takes Sundays off. My partner drives a bus, so it wouldn't just be me losing work.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent, food and the car straight away. Goes to every union meeting and protest, writes to her member of parliament for the first time, and when the job goes, applies for support and leans on her mother's spare room if they lose the cottage.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, doing sums that don't work. She also feels she has to hide it from her partner.
S2.quote: Four months of savings sounds like a lot until you've got two of you with no wage.
S2.fieldNote: Beth's resistance shows clearly here: her answer to a sudden shock is protest and support, not new skills. The double hit, with her partner's bus job also at risk, is what makes this frightening rather than just the farm. She'd hide her fear from Tomás, whom she describes as the more adaptable of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before but louder and earlier. I'd say this is the time to get rules in place, like a tax on every robot that replaces a worker, and money for people to live on. I'd try to get the union to run meetings in the villages, not just in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years only changes how long I'd be dreading it. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, and I still wouldn't know how to do anything but farm. The extra time helps the people who are good at reinventing themselves, and that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd save hard, maybe get us to six months put by, and I'd stand for the union's branch committee, which I've been avoiding. I might do the hoof-trimming and AI-insemination tickets, because they're the hands-on jobs I think would go last. When it actually arrives, I'd probably do what I said before: fight, apply for support, and lean on family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, rather than in a panic. It's like seeing a storm on the forecast for next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the time helps others more than you. Is there anything that would make you use those five years differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone paid me to learn, and it was proper hands-on training with a real job at the end, I might. But I'm not paying out of my own savings to learn computers on the chance it works out. I've seen that course in the county town, and it's all screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned AI insemination. For anyone reading, what's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's nothing to do with computers, funnily enough. AI there means artificial insemination, putting the bull's semen in the cow yourself instead of keeping a bull. It's fiddly work that takes a good hand and a calm cow, and I'm decent at it.

S3.say: I'd say now's the time to get rules in, like a tax on every robot that replaces a worker, and money for people to live on. I'd push the union to hold meetings in the villages.
S3.think: Five years only changes how long I'd be dreading it. I'd be thirty-two with nothing but farming, and the extra time helps people who are good at reinventing themselves, which isn't me.
S3.do: Saves hard to reach about six months of expenses and stands for the union branch committee in the first two years. Takes the hoof-trimming and artificial insemination certificates as the hands-on skills likely to go last, then fights, applies for support and leans on family when it arrives.
S3.feel: Anxious but not panicked, like a storm on next week's forecast.
S3.quote: Five years only changes how long I'd be dreading it.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time gives Beth more chance to organise and save, but not a different plan. She'd only retrain if someone else paid and the course was hands-on; screen-based courses put her off. Her joke about the two meanings of AI showed real pride in her skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say we've got no excuse not to get it right. Unions, councils, the government, they've got a decade to sort out wages and housing for people who lose their jobs. I'd be the one in the pub saying don't let them tell you it's natural, somebody chose this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest with myself, ten years is long enough that I couldn't pretend it wasn't coming. I'd be thirty-seven. That's young enough to start again, which is the scary bit, because then the only thing stopping me is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still stay at Ridge as long as there's milking to do, maybe five or six years. I'd save steadily and get on the union committee, and somewhere in the middle I'd probably make myself do a course, maybe something like care work or a job looking after animals that still need a person, like at the vet's or a rescue farm. I'd want Tomás and me to have a plan for the bus too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. It's further off, and I'd have time, but there's a nagging feeling under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd never train your replacement. With ten years, would you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if I'm honest, and I don't love saying it. If it's definitely coming, then refusing to learn is just me being stubborn for nothing. I'd rather learn something that's mine, though, like animal care, than babysit Mr Hollins's robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, because she's been through a factory closing. She worked at the dairy plant in town till it shut, and she says the worst bit was everybody pretending it wasn't happening until the last month. She'd tell me to stop moaning and start planning, and she'd be right.

S4.say: I'd say with ten years there's no excuse not to get it right, and governments, councils and unions should sort out wages and housing now. I'd keep telling people it isn't natural, somebody chose this.
S4.think: Ten years is long enough that I couldn't pretend it wasn't coming. At thirty-seven I'd be young enough to start again, so the only thing stopping me would be me.
S4.do: Stays at Ridge Farm while milking lasts, perhaps five or six years, saving steadily and joining the union committee. Partway through, makes herself take a course in animal care or a similar hands-on field, and plans with her partner for his bus job too.
S4.feel: Mostly uneasy, with time on her side but a nagging feeling underneath.
S4.quote: That's young enough to start again, which is the scary bit, because then the only thing stopping me is me.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year version is the only one where Beth admits her stubbornness could be the problem. She still wants to stay in work with animals and would rather learn animal care than look after robots. Her mother's experience of the dairy plant closing shapes how she thinks about warning time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily, because there's no time to do anything except panic and protest. What would help is the government making the companies that sell the robots pay into a fund, so people like me and Tomás get a wage while we find our feet. And proper paid training that's done with your hands, not on a screen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about the workers, and fair enough, but a robot can't tell a cow's off her food because she's grieving her calf. I'm not saying that saves my job. I'm just saying somebody should still be noticing.

headlineQuote: A robot can't tell a cow's off her food because she's grieving her calf.
portrait: Beth Garcia is 27 and has milked and fed about 140 cows at Ridge Farm for eight years, living in a rented village cottage with her partner Tomás, a school bus driver. She's a committed union member who has never used AI tools and sees the technology as something sold to farm owners to need fewer workers. A plateau leaves her calm and a little smug, but steady change brings real fear because robot milkers already exist nearby. In the fast AGI picture she turns to protest, politics and family, worried as much for Tomás's job as her own. Only with ten years' warning does she admit that her own stubbornness might be what holds her back, and talks about retraining in hands-on animal care.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because there would be no time to do anything except panic and protest, and both she and her partner could lose their jobs.
whatWouldHelp: A fund paid for by the companies selling robots that gives displaced workers a wage while they find their feet, and paid training that's hands-on rather than on a screen.
